subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: ATP is used as the immediate energy source in cells because:
choices: It stores very large amounts of energy for long-term use
It can be transported easily between cells in the blood plasma
It releases energy in small, usable amounts and is easily regenerated
It is the only molecule that contains phosphate groups
items.note: ATP → ADP + Pi releases a manageable amount of energy; ATP is soluble, moves within cells and is quickly re-made by respiration. It is not a long-term store.

items.stem: Which is a product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
choices: Ethanol
Lactate
Oxygen
Glycerol
items.note: Humans make lactate; yeast makes ethanol and CO₂. Anaerobic respiration yields only 2 ATP per glucose (from glycolysis).

items.stem: Cell respiration differs from gas exchange because respiration:
choices: Is a set of enzyme-controlled reactions that release energy inside cells
Is the movement of air into and out of the lungs by ventilation muscles
Is the diffusion of oxygen across the alveolar wall
Only happens in organisms with lungs
items.note: Respiration is a cellular chemical process; ventilation and gas exchange supply its oxygen and remove its CO₂.

items.stem: In a respirometer, the soda lime / KOH is included to:
choices: Supply oxygen for the organisms to respire
Keep the temperature inside the respirometer constant throughout
Kill microorganisms on the surface of seeds
Absorb carbon dioxide so volume change shows oxygen uptake
items.note: With CO₂ absorbed, the fall in gas volume equals the O₂ used — the coloured liquid moves towards the organisms.

items.stem: The main reason aerobic respiration produces much more ATP than anaerobic respiration is that:
choices: Glycolysis happens twice as fast when oxygen is present
Oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor
Anaerobic respiration uses up ATP to make lactate
Aerobic respiration breaks down twice as many glucose molecules per minute as anaerobic
items.note: Glycolysis gives 2 ATP either way; with oxygen, pyruvate is fully oxidised and the electron transport chain makes most of the ATP (about 30+).

choices: Cytoplasm
Mitochondrial matrix
Inner mitochondrial membrane
Intermembrane space
items.note: Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm; the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix; the ETC on the cristae.

items.stem: In the link reaction, pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA. This involves:
choices: Phosphorylation of pyruvate using two ATP
Reduction of pyruvate to lactate
Splitting each pyruvate into two molecules of glycerate phosphate
Decarboxylation and oxidation, producing CO₂ and reduced NAD
items.note: Pyruvate loses CO₂ (decarboxylation) and hydrogen (oxidation, reducing NAD); the acetyl group joins coenzyme A.

items.stem: During chemiosmosis, ATP synthase makes ATP using energy from:
choices: Electrons passing directly through ATP synthase
Oxygen reacting with hydrogen inside ATP synthase
Protons diffusing back into the matrix down their gradient
Hydrolysis of glucose molecules in the intermembrane space
items.note: The ETC pumps protons into the intermembrane space; their flow back through ATP synthase drives ATP formation.

items.stem: Why does the electron transport chain stop if oxygen is absent?
choices: No final electron acceptor removes electrons, so carriers stay reduced
Oxygen is needed to make the carriers in the chain
Protons can only cross the inner membrane when oxygen is also present there
ATP synthase is made of oxygen-containing amino acids
items.note: Oxygen accepts electrons and protons to form water. Without it, the chain backs up, NAD is not regenerated and the Krebs cycle stops.

items.stem: Per molecule of glucose, the Krebs cycle turns:
choices: Once, because one glucose enters the cycle
Four times, once for each carbon atom
Six times, once for each carbon atom in glucose
Twice, because glycolysis produces two pyruvate
items.note: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate → 2 acetyl CoA → 2 turns of the cycle.

items.stem: Lipids yield more energy per gram than carbohydrates in respiration mainly because:
choices: Lipids are respired anaerobically to make more ATP
Lipids bypass the electron transport chain completely
Fatty acids contain more C–H bonds and less oxygen per gram
Glycerol is converted directly into ATP
items.note: More hydrogen per gram means more reduced NAD/FAD and so more ATP from the ETC. Fatty acids enter as acetyl CoA after β-oxidation (no glycolysis).

items.stem: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans.
markscheme: Both start with glycolysis / produce pyruvate / produce ATP (1)
Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not (1)
Aerobic produces CO₂ and water; anaerobic produces lactate (1)
Aerobic yields much more ATP per glucose (about 30+) than anaerobic (2)
Aerobic involves mitochondria; anaerobic is in the cytoplasm only (1)
items.tactic: Compare = at least one similarity plus differences side by side.

items.stem: Outline why anaerobic respiration in yeast is used in baking and brewing.
markscheme: Yeast converts glucose to ethanol and CO₂ without oxygen (1)
Ethanol is the alcohol produced in brewing (1)
Ethanol in bread evaporates during baking (1)
items.tactic: Applications: name the product and say why it is useful in each case.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of the mitochondrion is adapted to its function in aerobic respiration.
markscheme: Cristae (folded inner membrane) give a large surface area for ETC and ATP synthase (1)
Small intermembrane space so a high proton concentration builds quickly (1)
Matrix contains enzymes for the link reaction and Krebs cycle (1)
Inner membrane impermeable to protons except through ATP synthase (1)
Own DNA/ribosomes to make some proteins (1)
items.tactic: Structure–function: each structure plus how it helps.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Germinating seeds were placed in a respirometer with KOH at 25 °C (invented data). The coloured liquid moved 32 mm in 20 min. The capillary tube has a cross-sectional area of 0.80 mm².
(a) Calculate the volume of oxygen used. (b) Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. (c) Explain why the liquid moved towards the seeds. (d) Suggest a control for this experiment.
markscheme: (c) Seeds take in O₂; CO₂ produced is absorbed by KOH, so gas volume/pressure falls (1)
(d) Same set-up with glass beads / boiled (dead) seeds of equal volume (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
